slide_text: The Encoder-Decoder Pipeline — A Real Data Engineering Problem You are handed a real task at work: We bought a recommendation engine . It reads a CSV file with three columns — — and writes its recommendations to another CSV with columns . It only accepts integers for . Our data, however, identifies users by email address : [code block] Make it work. And when the engine answers, translate its output back to emails. You cannot change the engine. So you will wrap it: [code block] The Encoder and Decoder are separate programs that communicate only through files — so the mapping between emails and integers must itself be saved to a file. This pattern (encode → black box → decode) is everywhere: ML pipelines call it label encoding , and you already met its purest form in the Information Theory chapter. Part 2: The Encoder

Each time you see a user for the first time, add them with the next integer as their ID. Hint 2 Check first. Quick Check 2.1 — What Does build_mapping Guarantee? Which of the following best describes what guarantees? A. Every email gets a random integer B. Every email gets a unique integer, and the same email always maps to the same integer C. Emails are sorted alphabetically before assigning IDs D. The mapping is stored in a file automatically Answer: B — The check means a user only gets an ID once, and it never changes. Every distinct user gets a different number. This one-to-one property is what makes the mapping safely invertible later.

Part 4: The Decoder

Invert the Mapping The mapping file maps email → id. The decoder needs id → email. Write . (You built this in the Dictionaries chapter — rebuild it from memory.) Why is inversion safe here — what property must the mapping have? [code block] Hint 1 Create a new dictionary where each old value becomes a key and each old key becomes a value. In other words, flip every pair around. Hint 2 does it in one line. Inversion is safe when all values are unique — if two emails shared the same integer, one would overwrite the other. Quick Check 4.1 — Why Encode at All? The recommendation engine takes integer IDs instead of email addresses. Why is this encoding step necessary? A. Emails take too much memory — integers are smaller B. The recommendation algorithm uses math operations (like computing averages and similarity scores) that require numbers, not text C. Python can't compare strings, only numbers D. Encoding makes the data more secure by hiding email addresses Answer: B — The engine does arithmetic on user IDs (averages, similarity scores). Strings cannot be added or averaged. Option A has a grain of truth but is not the reason the engine requires integers. C is false (Python compares strings just fine), and D is a side effect, not the purpose.

Quick Check 5.1 — What Could Go Wrong? If two different emails accidentally received the same integer ID, what would happen when you invert the mapping? A. Python would raise an error B. One email would silently overwrite the other — some recommendations would go to the wrong person C. The recommender would crash D. Nothing — duplicate IDs are fine Answer: B — When you invert a dictionary with duplicate values, the second key overwrites the first. So might become and Alice's recommendations would be lost. That is why 's one-to-one guarantee is so important.

Part 6: What You Just Invented The same encode → black box → decode shape appears everywhere in computing. Think of converting text to numbers before feeding a model, or compressing data before sending it over a network (your Huffman coder from the Information Theory chapter!). The black box changes; the wrapper pattern never does.

What You Just Invented What you built Its real name , — messy text to clean data Data parsing — every pipeline starts here — email → integer, first-seen order Label encoding — does exactly this , — mapping saved as a file Serialization — separate programs share data only through files — the Encoder program Adapter / wrapper — reshape your data to fit someone else's tool — untouched black box Black-box integration — you wrapped it instead of changing it , — the Decoder program Decoding / inverse mapping — translate answers back to the original form — end-to-end verification Integration testing — trust pipelines you have tested, not just ones that ran
Part 7: Reflection — What Did You Just Build?

Reflection Take a moment to answer these questions in your own words. Why can't the recommender just use email addresses directly? What does encoding actually solve? Why do the Encoder and Decoder need to save the mapping to a file, instead of just keeping it in a variable? What would go wrong if gave two different emails the same integer? How does your code prevent that? The pattern you built — encode, process, decode — shows up everywhere. Can you think of another example from everyday life where something gets converted to a different form, processed, and then converted back? (Think about languages, zip files, or even cooking recipes.) What is one thing you would add to to make it even more thorough?
